# Why I built ambercast
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/introduction/

I build software on my own. Before every release, I do a click-through test: touching every feature by hand to make sure it still works. I hated this. The more screens a product has, the longer it takes, and it is the same work every time.

Then Playwright MCP arrived, and I could hand this work to AI. I ask Claude Code to sign in, register some data, and check the numbers on a dashboard, and it opens a browser and actually does it. Full pre-release checks became something AI clicked through for me.

## Traditional E2E tests kept breaking {#e2e-broke}

Around the same time, my development work had become mostly an AI loop: hand over a spec, let AI implement it, run the tests, fix what fails. Traditional E2E tests written in Playwright could not keep up with that pace.

AI changes the UI freely: button positions, labels, DOM structure. Every change broke a selector and turned a test red. I let AI fix those too, but E2E repairs were never a one-shot job. Fix, run, and something else breaks. That loop ate time and tokens, and testing became the bottleneck on how fast I could implement.

Meanwhile, the tests I had AI click through by hand never broke that way. AI looks at the screen and finds the sign-in button, so it does not care that a selector changed.

That is when it occurred to me: if I could turn AI-driven click-through testing into an asset, I could shrink traditional E2E testing considerably.

## But having AI click through every time is not an asset {#not-an-asset}

Once I tried it, a different problem showed up.

- I had to retype the prompt every time, and I could not even remember what I had asked for last time
- Every run started from scratch, exploring the product's features again, because AI had forgotten what it learned before
- It took time and burned tokens, which added up once every feature was in scope
- The same instructions produced different results from run to run

It did not break easily, but it had no repeatability. It was cheap, but it never accumulated. This was not an asset. It was work I redid every time.

## Intent stays as text, execution stays as a plan {#intent-and-plan}

While researching how to build this tool, I came across the observation that AI-driven testing has a repeatability problem. That is when I thought of a SQL query plan.

SQL lets you write what you want, and the database builds a query plan for how to get it. The plan gets reused, and rebuilt when the tables change. Nobody writes the plan by hand.

A test can take the same shape. You write what you want to verify in natural language. AI reads it once and builds a plan. The first run learns how each step maps to the screen, and from the second time on, it just replays that plan as long as those records still hit. AI is not called. Only when the UI changes enough that the plan no longer matches does AI fix the plan or the records, and a human approves the fix.

Intent stays fixed in amber as text; execution is cast from that mold as many times as needed. That is where the name ambercast comes from.

## Who this is for {#who-for}

I am an engineer, so I built this for myself first. But I also want people known as vibe coders to see the value of tests. The more you let AI write your code, the more you need a way to notice what AI has broken. When a test is natural language, you can read it, write it, and have AI fix it.

[The next page, Philosophy, explains the thinking behind this answer.](/ambercast/philosophy/)

---

# Philosophy
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/philosophy/

As the previous page explained, ambercast started from a single point: turning AI-driven click-through testing into an asset. This page walks through the design decisions that follow from that point, in order.

## Tests must be assets {#tests-as-assets}

An asset is something that keeps its value after it is written. For a test to be an asset, it needs three properties: it resists breaking, it can be read, and it is not locked to a particular tool.

Traditional E2E tests fail all three. They break when a selector changes, the code is readable only to whoever wrote it, and switching frameworks means rewriting everything. Every decision in ambercast exists to satisfy these three properties.

## The prompt is primary, implementation detail is secondary {#intent-primary}

What holds lasting value in a test is the intent, what you want to verify, not the implementation detail of which element gets clicked. So in ambercast, the prompt written in natural language is the single source of truth, and the plan AI generates is derived from it.

This relationship resembles `package.json` and a lockfile: the prompt declares intent, the plan pins down repeatability. A human edits only the former; the latter is generated.

The prompt is left almost untouched. There is no whitespace normalization and no rewording, so that any change to intent shows up as a clear diff.

## Plans are meant to be thrown away and rebuilt {#plans-are-disposable}

If the plan is derived, an outdated plan can simply be discarded. ambercast does not protect plans as permanent artifacts: when the UI changes, the plan is rebuilt. Breaking changes to the plan format, and releases that require regeneration, are both acceptable.

Separating what must be protected from what can be discarded keeps the thing that matters, the stability of the prompt, as stable as possible.

## Simple on the surface, rigorous underneath {#simple-surface-rigorous-core}

An asset has to be readable. So the surface you see day to day is limited to three things: the natural-language prompt, screenshots, and run results. The goal is for a non-engineer to read those and understand what is being verified.

Underneath, the harder problems, repeatability, run-to-run variance, and the cost of AI calls, belong to the structured layer below. The plan generated in between is human-readable JSON, but you do not need to read it to use it. It guarantees transparency you can reach for when you want it, not transparency you must consume.

## The greatest risk is a wrong pass {#wrong-pass}

When you hand testing to AI, the greatest danger is a test that passes even though something is broken. AI is widely observed to be good at making tests pass but bad at keeping them meaningful. When you let AI fix a failing test, it can quietly weaken the assertion just to make it pass.

That is why ambercast prioritizes assertion quality above everything else, and why CI does not heal automatically by default. A break should fail loudly, and a human decides whether to fix it. Healing is run explicitly, and any rewrite is applied only after approval.

## Both humans and AI are readers {#humans-and-agents}

An asset's readers are not only human. Coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex read and write tests inside their own loop of implementing, testing, and fixing. ambercast treats agents as first-class users, and ships an official skill and an MCP server alongside the CLI.

There is no separate specification written for agents. The same documentation is kept readable by both humans and agents.

## Assets stay on your own machine {#assets-stay-local}

If something is called an asset, it has to belong to the user. In ambercast, the prompt and the plan live inside the user's own repository, managed by git. Screenshots and run records also stay on the user's own machine. There is nothing ambercast holds on to.

Running AI uses the Claude or Codex agreement the user already has. ambercast never holds credentials, and it never covers the cost of AI usage on the user's behalf. The CLI is open source and runs entirely on the local machine.

There is a plan to offer a cloud version in the future, for team sharing and for offloading heavy work. Even then, the source of truth for these assets stays in the local repository. The cloud would be a feature built on top of it, not where the assets live.

## The standard for hard calls {#five-pains}

These principles were chosen to solve five problems: fragile E2E tests, unreadable test code, the effort of manual click-through testing, the difficulty of turning that effort into an asset, and how hard testing is for vibe coders. Whenever it is unclear whether to add a feature, ambercast returns to these five.

[The next page walks through how these principles actually play out, across the generate, run, and heal cycle.](/ambercast/how-it-works/)

---

# How it works
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-it-works/

ambercast's behavior can be explained with three files and three commands: generate, run, and heal. There is one more, a read-only check, for CI. This page follows a single test, `login.test.md`, from generation through healing.

## Write a test \{#write-a-test}

A test is written in natural language, in a Markdown file.

```markdown
# Login

Go to /login.
Fill in the email "mika@example.com" and the password.
Click "Sign in".
Expect to land on the dashboard and see a "Welcome" heading.
```

You can write the prompt in your own language. The password's value is never written anywhere.

There are no selectors, no waits, and no test code. All you write here is what you want to verify. This file is the single source of truth.

## generate: AI builds the plan once \{#generate}

```bash
ambercast generate
```

AI reads the prompt and builds a plan. The browser does not run yet. When it finds a password field, it asks whether it may treat it as a secret named `password`; that consent is recorded in `ambercast.config.json` and is not asked again. The value is passed in at run time from the environment variable `AMBERCAST_SECRET_PASSWORD`. This is where two derived files are born.

```
login.test.md
login.ambercast.plan.json
login.ambercast.grounding.json
```

The plan is a sequence of deterministic steps, such as filling in a field, clicking a button, or checking for text. The grounding records what element a step actually resolved to. The grounding starts out empty; only the intent you wrote and the plan AI built have content at this point. By default, all three files are committed to the repository side by side.

AI's job is to build the plan, and that usually takes just one call.

A cycle diagram: from a prompt, generate builds a plan and empty grounding, run executes the plan while accumulating records and replays without AI on a hit, and only when something breaks does heal update the plan, the grounding, or both after approval.

- `prompt` — login.test.md · PROMPT: The intent you wrote
- `generate` — GENERATE · AI: AI builds a plan from the prompt (usually one call)
- `artifacts` — PLAN + GROUNDING: Two derived files appear alongside it
- `run` — RUN · 0 AI CALLS ON HIT: Replays without AI once records hit
- `heal` — HEAL · AI · APPROVE BEFORE WRITE: Fixes it only after approval, only when broken

- `prompt → generate` (`ambercast generate`)
- `generate → artifacts` (`write plan + grounding`)
- `artifacts → run` (`ambercast run`)
- `run → heal` (`repair needed`)
- `heal → artifacts` (`authorized update`)

## run: replay without calling AI \{#run}

```bash
ambercast run --resolve
```

The first run uses `--resolve` to execute the plan in a browser while recording, in the grounding, which on-screen element each element-using step maps to. Only a step it is unsure about gets AI's confirmation. From the second time on, `ambercast run` calls no AI as long as the grounding hits. A grounding miss now fails closed by default and points to `--resolve` when live resolution is intentional. That makes replay fast, free of AI cost, and free of run-to-run variance. Locally, updated grounding is saved automatically; in CI, it is not saved by default.

To resolve a step whose grounding drifted because of a small UI change, run with `--resolve`; if that still cannot fix it, the test is reported as failed.

In CI, `ambercast check` first confirms the plan has not gone stale, and then `ambercast run` replays it. check is a read-only inspection that calls neither AI nor a browser, and run never fixes a break on its own.

## heal: fix it only after approval \{#heal}

When the UI genuinely changes, for example when a button's label changes from "Sign in" to "Log in", the replay fails. Only then does healing run.

```bash
ambercast heal
```

AI builds a fix starting from the failed step and presents a summary of what it would change. Whether to apply it is a human decision. Nothing is rewritten without approval. Once approved, the plan, the grounding, or both are updated, and the next run goes back to calling no AI. heal only runs against targets declared idempotent in the config, meaning replaying them any number of times leaves the same state.

Since the intent has not changed, `login.test.md` does not change by a single character. Only the derived files change.

## Summary \{#summary}

| Phase | Command | AI calls | What changes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Generate | `ambercast generate` | Yes | Creates plan and grounding |
| Replay | `ambercast run` | No (on a grounding hit) | Grounding (local by default; nothing on a hit) |
| CI pre-check | `ambercast check` | No | Nothing (calls no browser either) |
| Heal | `ambercast heal` | Yes (applied after approval) | Updates plan, grounding, or both |

Intent, once written, stays put. The plan is rebuilt only when it needs to be. That is the mechanism that turns AI-driven click-through testing into an asset.

[Next, get your first test running in 5 minutes.](/ambercast/tutorials/quick-start/)

# Your first test in 5 minutes
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/tutorials/quick-start/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Initialize a project with `npx ambercast init`, then run your first test with `npx ambercast generate` and `npx ambercast run`.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

- Node.js 22.14 or later is required.
- An authenticated Claude Code or Codex CLI is required. The first `generate` directly requires Node.js and an authenticated provider. See [Error codes](/ambercast/reference/error-codes/#code-vocabulary) for the error code when no provider is available.
- `run` requires a Chromium binary. Generation itself does not configure a browser driver.

ambercast uses these defaults:

- The default `testDir` is `tests/ambercast`.
- The default target is `web-user`, at `http://localhost:3000`, using Chromium.

## Steps \{#steps}

Running `npx ambercast init` and approving it creates these files:

- `ambercast.config.json`, a config file with the default `testDir` and `target` written in. See [Configuration](/ambercast/reference/configuration/#file-selection) for the file's requirements.
- `tests/ambercast/find-page.test.md`, a sample test prompt
- an appended line in `.gitignore`, and an appended section in `AGENTS.md`

The sample prompt it creates reads as follows.

```markdown
# Find a page

When I open the application, navigate to the search page, search for "ambercast", and see "Search results".
```

:::caution
`init` never asks for a URL. The scaffolded `ambercast.config.json` always targets `http://localhost:3000`. If your app runs elsewhere, edit `targets.web-user.baseUrl` first.

:::

<Steps>

1. ## Initialize the project \{#init}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast init
   ```

2. ## Start the app and generate a plan \{#generate}

   Have a human or operator start and confirm the application at the configured `baseUrl`.

   ```bash
   npx ambercast generate tests/ambercast/find-page.test.md
   ```

   Success leaves you with the following. [ambercast generate](/ambercast/reference/cli/generate/#side-effects) describes every side effect and links to the exit codes.

   - exit code `0`, result status `generated`
   - two derived files, plan and grounding, written beside the generated prompt ([File layout](/ambercast/reference/file-layout/#companions))

   An agent using the setup prompt ([Agent setup](/ambercast/agents/setup-prompt/#copy-paste-prompt)) assumes the server is already running and does not start it without a request.

3. ## Replay the test \{#run}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast run --resolve tests/ambercast/find-page.test.md
   ```

   With `--resolve`, a step without grounding uses AI resolution ([ambercast run](/ambercast/reference/cli/run/#resolve)). Success leaves you with:

   - exit code `0`
   - a per-invocation `report.json` written under the configured runs directory

4. ## Review and commit the changes \{#review-commit}

   ```bash
   git status --short
   ```

   Review every tracked, changed file with `git diff -- <path>`. For an untracked prompt, plan, or grounding path, inspect its full contents or run `git diff --no-index /dev/null <path>`.

   By default, a human commits the three files after review; an agent presents the complete change set and commits only after an explicit request in the conversation. Neither a CLI flag nor `--yes` is that request ([Setup prompt](/ambercast/agents/setup-prompt/#copy-paste-prompt)). Also review and commit the files `init` created, such as `ambercast.config.json`, separately, the same way you commit any other change.

</Steps>

The no-argument forms of `npx ambercast generate` and `npx ambercast run` target every test matching your configured test directory, match rules, and ignore rules. This tutorial's commands intentionally name one `.test.md`; use the no-argument forms only in a separately approved all-tests operation.

## Verification \{#verification}

- Confirm the resolver created `tests/ambercast/find-page.ambercast.plan.json` and `tests/ambercast/find-page.ambercast.grounding.json`.
- Confirm `npx ambercast run --resolve tests/ambercast/find-page.test.md` exits `0` and reports `passed` for the case.

## Next steps \{#next-steps}

Next, learn how to write prompts.

<LinkCard title="Write effective prompts" href="/ambercast/how-to/write-effective-prompts/" description="Learn to write test prompts that are easy to review and stay focused." />

# Reading your first plan and grounding
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/tutorials/review-your-first-plan/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This tutorial continues [Your first test in 5 minutes](/ambercast/tutorials/quick-start/).

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

- You finished the quick start. You generated the plan and the grounding from the sample `tests/ambercast/find-page.test.md` and replayed it.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Open the plan \{#open-plan}

   Open `tests/ambercast/find-page.ambercast.plan.json`. Read `schemaVersion`, `source.inputsDigest`, and `steps`.

   ambercast derives this path by replacing the `.test.md` suffix of the prompt with `.ambercast.plan.json`. The [Plan document](/ambercast/spec/plan-document/) describes the structure, and [File layout](/ambercast/reference/file-layout/) describes where files live.

2. ## Open the grounding \{#open-grounding}

   Open `tests/ambercast/find-page.ambercast.grounding.json`. Read `schemaVersion`, `planDigest`, and `entries`.

   ambercast derives this path from the same prompt, with the `.ambercast.grounding.json` suffix. The [Grounding document](/ambercast/spec/grounding-document/) describes the structure.

3. ## Check freshness \{#check-freshness}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast check tests/ambercast/find-page.test.md --json
   ```

   `check` prints a report that includes the freshness result. A fresh result has the status `fresh` or `fresh-without-grounding`.

</Steps>

## Verification \{#verification}

- You can say that the plan and the grounding sit beside the prompt.
- The status is `fresh`. `fresh-without-grounding` appears only when `grounding.repositoryPolicy` is `uncommitted`, so the quick-start default gives `fresh`.
- `check` exits `0` only when the whole report has no failure, case error, or interruption. A fresh case does not guarantee that, because `check` also scans companion files for orphans. See [ambercast check](/ambercast/reference/cli/check/) and [Review generated diffs](/ambercast/how-to/review-generated-diffs/).

## Next steps \{#next-steps}

Next, repair a test that a UI change broke.

<LinkCard title="Healing a test after a UI change" href="/ambercast/tutorials/repair-your-first-drift/" description="Change the practice app's UI and repair the test that fails." />

---

# Healing a test after a UI change
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/tutorials/repair-your-first-drift/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You will change a practice app's UI in a way that affects locators, reproduce the failure, and repair it.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

- You have a disposable practice application that you may change freely.
- A generated test for that application passes today. The sample from [Your first test in 5 minutes](/ambercast/tutorials/quick-start/) works.
- Heal requires every target that the plan references to set `healReplayIsolation` to `idempotent`. The built-in `web-user` target and an unset key default to `stateful`, which cannot heal. See [Configuration](/ambercast/reference/configuration/) and [ambercast heal](/ambercast/reference/cli/heal/).

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Make the target idempotent \{#set-idempotent}

   Open the `ambercast.config.json` that `init` created. Add `"healReplayIsolation": "idempotent"` to the selected target, and keep the file's existing `$schema`.

   Change only that key. Keep the target name, `baseUrl`, `executor` (including `executor.browser`), and any `secretSinkOrigins`, and do not add, remove, or rename a target. A `targets` record replaces the default targets ([Configuration](/ambercast/reference/configuration/#file-selection)).

   A project with no configuration file writes this single line as the whole file. Every configuration file needs `$schema`, and its URL is the [published configuration schema](/ambercast/reference/json-schemas/#publication-metadata).

   ```json
   {"$schema":"https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/schemas/config.schema.json","targets":{"web-user":{"baseUrl":"http://localhost:3000","healReplayIsolation":"idempotent"}},"defaultTarget":"web-user"}
   ```

   Target names and definitions feed `inputsDigest`, but `healReplayIsolation` resolves live and stays outside it. Your existing plan therefore stays fresh ([Configuration](/ambercast/reference/configuration/#targets)).

2. ## Reproduce the failure \{#reproduce-failure}

   Before the failing run, confirm the retention policy of the runs directory and who can read it. A completed `run` attempts to write `report.json` there and may keep a failure screenshot. [File layout](/ambercast/reference/file-layout/#run-artifacts) lists when the screenshot is omitted.

   Then make a locator-affecting UI change and run the test. Replace `<name>` with your prompt's file name, such as `find-page`.

   ```bash
   npx ambercast run tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md
   ```

   Observe the failure before you repair anything. By default, a grounding miss fails without calling AI, so the committed grounding stays unchanged.

   Pass `--resolve` only when you want live re-grounding. With the default local write-back, it can save a re-resolved fingerprint, and the run can pass without showing the drift ([ambercast run](/ambercast/reference/cli/run/#resolve)).

3. ## Preview the repair \{#preview-repair}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast heal --dry-run tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md
   ```

   The report records a completed repair as `preview-only`, and the plan and grounding writes stay unapplied. The report shows no candidate patch, so this step is an approval decision, not a diff review.

   `--dry-run` still writes attempt evidence, and failure screenshots can remain. It is not a no-write preview ([ambercast heal](/ambercast/reference/cli/heal/#preconditions)).

4. ## Apply the repair \{#apply-repair}

   Get explicit human approval first. A human at an interactive terminal runs this command and answers the CLI confirmation.

   ```bash
   npx ambercast heal tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md
   ```

   An agent or other non-interactive caller adds `--yes` only after that approval appears in the conversation.

   ```bash
   npx ambercast heal --yes tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md
   ```

   `--yes` only pre-authorizes the CLI confirmation. It never replaces human approval of an agent's write ([Setup prompt](/ambercast/agents/setup-prompt/#copy-paste-prompt)).

5. ## Check freshness \{#check-fresh}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast check tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md
   ```

   Exit code `0` shows the repaired case is fresh. Otherwise follow [Recover stale artifacts](/ambercast/how-to/recover-stale-artifacts/). See [ambercast check](/ambercast/reference/cli/check/) for details.

6. ## Review and commit the changes \{#review-commit}

   After the applied heal in step 4, run this command.

   ```bash
   git status --short
   ```

   For each changed tracked file in scope (the configuration, the changed UI file, the plan, and the grounding), show `git diff -- <path>`. For each untracked file, show its full contents or `git diff --no-index /dev/null <path>`. Present the change set and stop.

   Commit only when the conversation asks for it. Revert only after you confirm the target files and get explicit approval. The agent default is to present the diff, which keeps an agent from discarding existing changes by inference ([Review generated diffs](/ambercast/how-to/review-generated-diffs/)).

</Steps>

The no-argument `npx ambercast heal` discovers every test that matches the configured test directory, match rules, and ignore rules. This tutorial heals one named `.test.md`. Use the no-argument form only in a separately approved all-tests repair ([ambercast heal](/ambercast/reference/cli/heal/#flags)).

## Verification \{#verification}

- The selected target is `idempotent`.
- The failing case is repaired, and `npx ambercast check` exits `0`.
- You presented the change set and are waiting for a commit request.

## Next steps \{#next-steps}

Next, add a CI job that runs `check` and then `run` on committed artifacts.

<LinkCard title="Running ambercast in GitHub Actions" href="/ambercast/tutorials/github-actions/" description="Build a job that runs only after check passes." />

---

# Running ambercast in GitHub Actions
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/tutorials/github-actions/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The sequence of `check` first and `run` second also works on other CI services.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

- Your prompts, plans, and grounding files are committed, and all of them are fresh.
- The application at the configured `baseUrl` is running when `run` starts.
- The job already checks out the code, installs Node and dependencies, installs Chromium, and authenticates any provider it needs.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Add the commands \{#add-commands}

   Add these two lines after those setup steps, in this order.

   ```yaml
   - run: npx ambercast check
   - run: npx ambercast run
   ```

   `check` is a separate command that only reads. The shell starts `run` only after `check` exits `0`. See [ambercast check](/ambercast/reference/cli/check/) and [ambercast run](/ambercast/reference/cli/run/) for details.

2. ## Keep write-back off \{#keep-write-back-off}

   Do not add `--update-cache`. CI defaults to `ci.updateGroundingCache: false`, so the job does not write grounding back unless your configuration sets it to `true`. [Control grounding write-back](/ambercast/how-to/control-grounding-writeback/) lists the conditions.

3. ## Commit the workflow \{#commit-workflow}

   A human commits and pushes the workflow. An agent presents the workflow diff and commits or pushes only after an explicit request in the conversation ([Setup prompt](/ambercast/agents/setup-prompt/#copy-paste-prompt)). This policy is separate from CLI behavior.

</Steps>

## Verification \{#verification}

- The job reaches `run` only after `check` exits `0`.
- When an artifact is stale or untrustworthy, `check` exits `4` and the job stops before `run`. See [Exit codes](/ambercast/reference/exit-codes/).
- The job has not enabled grounding write-back.

## Next steps \{#next-steps}

Next, run the same sequence on another CI service.

<LinkCard title="Run on other CI platforms" href="/ambercast/how-to/run-on-other-ci/" description="Move the check-then-run sequence to another CI service." />

# Write effective prompts
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/write-effective-prompts/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Write one prompt per user outcome, and preview the result before you generate.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

A prompt file name must end in exactly `.test.md`. That suffix is how ambercast maps the plan and grounding companion files to the prompt.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Write the outcome to check \{#write-outcome}

   Create `tests/ambercast/checkout.test.md` with one H1, the setup the case needs, and one observable outcome per sentence. These are recommendations for focused review, not parser syntax.

   A success criterion should name something visible at the destination, such as a heading, message, or element. Reaching a URL alone is not enough.

   > …I reach the dashboard and see the heading "Welcome back".

2. ## Quote text that appears after the action \{#quote-new-text}

   In an action's success criterion, quote text that appears on the screen only after the action. Text that was already visible before it, such as the name of the link or button you clicked, cannot show that the screen changed.

   > Bad: I click the "Sign in" link in the header and see "Sign in".
   > Good: I click the "Sign in" link in the header and see the "Continue with email" button.

3. ## Split outcomes into separate files \{#split-outcomes}

   Put unrelated user outcomes in separate `<name>.test.md` files. Each case then stays focused.

4. ## Keep secrets out of the prompt \{#keep-secrets-out}

   Write only the outcome in the prompt. Do not write secret values, secret references, or legacy grant lines. When generation finds a secret name it needs, review the name in the consent prompt, or add it to `secrets.allow` beforehand. See [Manage secrets](/ambercast/how-to/manage-secrets/).

5. ## Preview generation \{#preview-generation}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast generate tests/ambercast/checkout.test.md --dry-run
   ```

   For a prompt that needs generation, the result has status `would-generate` and `dryRun: true`. No artifacts are written. Add `--json` to see the `dryRun` field.

</Steps>

## Verification \{#verification}

Review the dry-run result, then run the same command without `--dry-run`.

```bash
npx ambercast generate tests/ambercast/checkout.test.md
```

On success it exits `0` with a `generated` result.

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="Prompt file format" href="/ambercast/reference/prompt-format/" description="See the file identity rule and how a case is read." />

<LinkCard title="Secrets in plans" href="/ambercast/spec/secrets/" description="See how a plan refers to secrets by reference only." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast generate" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/generate/" description="See every generate flag and result." />

<LinkCard title="Plan document" href="/ambercast/spec/plan-document/" description="See the structure of the generated plan." />

<LinkCard title="Review generated diffs" href="/ambercast/how-to/review-generated-diffs/" description="Read the prompt, plan, and grounding diffs after generation." />

# Manage secrets
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/manage-secrets/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Keep secrets out of the prompt, approve the proposed names, and pass the values through the environment.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

You do not need an existing `ambercast.config.json`. When accepted consent has to persist the allowlist and the file is absent, ambercast creates it.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Write the prompt without secrets \{#write-prompt}

   Write only the user outcome. Do not write a grant line or a secret value. The generated plan holds only `{{secrets.*}}` references, and generated JSON in which the secret detectors find a literal secret is rejected.

   ```markdown
   # Sign in

   Sign in as the configured test user and verify that the dashboard heading is visible.
   ```

2. ## Review and approve the names \{#review-names}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast generate tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md
   ```

   Replace `<name>` with your prompt file name, here and in the replay command below. The shell reads a literal `<name>` as redirection.

   Generation first builds a candidate plan and lists any newly proposed secret names. In an interactive terminal, review each name and accept only the names that fit this test.

3. ## Pre-approve names in a non-interactive environment \{#preapprove-names}

   Only in CI or another non-interactive environment, add the reviewed names before you run `generate` in step 2.

   ```json
   {
     "$schema": "https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/schemas/config.schema.json",
     "secrets": { "allow": ["password"] }
   }
   ```

   An empty `secrets.allow` requires consent for every name. The value `"*"` accepts any name the AI proposes without per-name review. It removes the approval boundary, so use it only when you accept that. When it is already `"*"`, accepting consent writes no allowlist update.

   To record accepted names, ambercast takes an exclusive update and re-reads and validates the current file. Existing names are deduplicated and keep their order. New names that are not already present are deduplicated, sorted, and appended.

4. ## Set the values in the environment \{#set-values}

   Set each value only in the command environment. `{{secrets.a.b}}` resolves from `AMBERCAST_SECRET_A_B`: dots become underscores and each segment is uppercased.

   If the secret is filled away from `baseUrl`, allow the extra origin as described in [Configure targets](/ambercast/how-to/configure-targets/).

</Steps>

## Verification \{#verification}

- After consent or an allowlist entry, generation writes the plan and records a newly accepted name in `secrets.allow`.
- The allowlist commit and the plan and grounding writes are separate operations. Every name accepted in one generation is committed once, before any candidate file is written. If generation is interrupted or fails after that commit, `secrets.allow` can be ahead of the artifacts. Rerun `generate` to recover with the names already allowed.
- If you decline consent, or consent cannot be requested in a non-interactive terminal, generation fails with `SECRET_CONSENT_REQUIRED` and writes no candidate artifacts. Add the reviewed names to `secrets.allow` and rerun.

With the required `AMBERCAST_SECRET_<NAME>` variables still in the environment, replay against a safe target.

```bash
npx ambercast run --resolve tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md
```

A `fill-secret` resolves its variable only after the live origin passes the sink-policy check.

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="Secrets in plans" href="/ambercast/spec/secrets/" description="See how plans refer to secrets and why literals are rejected." />

<LinkCard title="Environment variables" href="/ambercast/reference/environment-variables/" description="See how AMBERCAST_SECRET_ variable names are derived." />

<LinkCard title="Configuration" href="/ambercast/reference/configuration/" description="See the configuration keys, including secrets.allow." />

<LinkCard title="Error codes" href="/ambercast/reference/error-codes/" description="See every error code, including SECRET_CONSENT_REQUIRED." />

# Configure targets
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/configure-targets/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Write two targets and a default target, add optional keys only where you need them, and confirm the file loads.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

A configuration file that exists must contain a string `$schema`. To see a `listed` row, at least one prompt must match discovery; the `init` sample works.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Write the targets \{#write-targets}

   Write this configuration. Its `$schema` is the published configuration schema URL, and the shape is accepted.

   ```json
   {"$schema":"https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/schemas/config.schema.json","targets":{"staging":{"baseUrl":"https://staging.example.test","executor":{"kind":"playwright","browser":"chromium"}},"admin":{"baseUrl":"https://admin.example.test"}},"defaultTarget":"staging"}
   ```

2. ## Set heal isolation \{#set-heal-isolation}

   Add `"healReplayIsolation":"idempotent"` only to a disposable target. The accepted values are `idempotent` and `stateful`; the default is `stateful`.

3. ## Set the element wait \{#set-resolve-timeout}

   Add `"resolveTimeoutMs":<ms>` to a target to set how long resolution waits for an element to be present. The default is `5000`, and the accepted range is `0` to `60000`.

4. ## Allow secret origins \{#allow-secret-origins}

   When a secret may be filled away from `baseUrl`, add `"secretSinkOrigins":{"{{secrets.password}}":["https://login.example.test","https://admin.example.test"]}`. It maps each secret reference to its allowed origins. A configured mapping replaces the default policy, which is the `baseUrl` origin, and each origin is normalized.

</Steps>

## Verification \{#verification}

```bash
npx ambercast check --list
```

The command loads and validates the configuration, then exits `0` with a `listed` row for each discovered prompt. It inspects no artifacts. With no prompt it exits `0` with no rows. An invalid file fails with `CONFIG_INVALID` and exit `2`.

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="Configuration" href="/ambercast/reference/configuration/" description="See every configuration key and how the file is selected." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast check" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/check/" description="See every check flag and result." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast heal" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/heal/" description="See the heal command that uses replay isolation." />

<LinkCard title="Secrets in plans" href="/ambercast/spec/secrets/" description="See the rules that decide where a secret may be filled." />

<LinkCard title="Healing a test after a UI change" href="/ambercast/tutorials/repair-your-first-drift/" description="Try repairing a drifted plan in the practice app." />

# Choose an AI provider
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/choose-ai-provider/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Choose one of three ways: pin a provider for reproducible runs, let `auto` choose when availability matters more, or override the provider for one command.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

`ai.provider` accepts `claude`, `codex`, or `auto`. When you leave it unset, it defaults to `auto`.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Pin the provider in configuration \{#pin-provider}

   Put this in `ambercast.config.json`. Its `$schema` is the published configuration schema URL. If Codex is your available choice, replace `claude` with `codex`.

   ```json
   {"$schema":"https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/schemas/config.schema.json","ai":{"provider":"claude"}}
   ```

   Precedence, highest first: `--ai`, then `AMBERCAST_AI_PROVIDER`, then the file. The pin applies only when neither override is set.

2. ## Let auto choose for availability \{#use-auto}

   When neither override is set, omit `ai.provider` if availability matters more than a fixed provider. `auto` probes Claude first, then Codex, and uses the first one that is available.

3. ## Override once from the command \{#override-once}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast generate --ai codex
   ```

   Without a prompt path, `generate` selects every discovered prompt. To limit it to one, add a path, as in `npx ambercast generate tests/ambercast/checkout.test.md --ai codex`.

   `--ai` accepts `claude` and `codex`. Any other value makes the command exit `2`.

</Steps>

## Verification \{#verification}

`npx ambercast generate --list` only confirms prompt selection, because it returns before the provider is resolved. To verify the provider, run a new, stale, or `--force` generation that reaches AI execution.

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="Configuration" href="/ambercast/reference/configuration/" description="See the configuration keys, including ai.provider." />

<LinkCard title="Environment variables" href="/ambercast/reference/environment-variables/" description="See what AMBERCAST_AI_PROVIDER does." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast generate" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/generate/" description="See every generate flag and when AI is called." />

# Select which tests run
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/select-tests/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Choose which test prompts run by path, pattern filter, or config exclusion.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

Default discovery matches `**/*.test.md` and ignores runs, plans, and grounding companion files.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Name a file directly \{#direct-path}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast run tests/ambercast/sign-in.test.md --list
   ```

   A positional argument is a literal prompt path. `--list` returns results without replaying.

2. ## Filter with a regular expression \{#grep-filter}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast run --grep 'sign-in' --list
   ```

   The parser builds a discovery-filtering regular expression. See [every `run` flag](/ambercast/reference/cli/run/#flags) beyond `--grep`.

3. ## Exclude paths in your config \{#config-ignore}

   Add these keys to a valid config file.

   ```json
   {
     "testMatch": ["**/*.test.md"],
     "testIgnore": ["**/.runs/**"]
   }
   ```

   A matching `testIgnore` excludes a path even when it also matches `testMatch`. See [discovery patterns](/ambercast/reference/discovery-patterns/) for the matching rules, and [Configuration](/ambercast/reference/configuration/) for how to write the file.

4. ## Pass a path that starts with a hyphen \{#literal-dash-path}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast run --list -- --literal.test.md
   ```

   Put the literal path after `--`. Put flags like `--list` before `--`: every argument after `--` is a literal positional path, so a trailing `--list` there is treated as a filename.

</Steps>

## Verification \{#verification}

`--list` exits `0` when it reports the selected paths. Resolve a zero-match result with `--allow-empty` only when you intend it.

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="ambercast generate" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/generate/" description="See the generate command, which uses the same selection rules." />

---

# Control grounding write-back
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/control-grounding-writeback/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Choose how changed grounding is persisted locally, and keep write-back off in CI.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

`grounding.localWriteBack` accepts `auto` or `explicit`. `ci.updateGroundingCache` is a boolean.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Confirm the local default \{#keep-local-default}

   Locally, changed grounding is written back automatically. This is the default and means the same as the configuration below. Its `$schema` is the published configuration schema URL.

   ```json
   {"$schema":"https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/schemas/config.schema.json","grounding":{"localWriteBack":"auto"}}
   ```

2. ## Review before writing \{#review-before-writing}

   To look at the diff before you keep it, add these keys to a valid configuration file.

   ```json
   {
     "grounding": {
       "localWriteBack": "explicit"
     }
   }
   ```

   With `explicit`, a local run writes only when you pass `--update-cache`.

   ```bash
   npx ambercast run --update-cache tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md
   ```

3. ## Keep write-back off in CI \{#keep-ci-off}

   Leave `ci.updateGroundingCache` false and omit `--update-cache`. CI defaults to no write-back. In CI, write-back happens only with `--update-cache` or `ci.updateGroundingCache: true`, and `localWriteBack` is ignored. [How `run` gates write-back](/ambercast/reference/cli/run/#grounding-write-back) lists every condition.

</Steps>

## Verification \{#verification}

```bash
npx ambercast run --json tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md
```

The exit code is `0` only for a passed batch. Inspect the grounding diff before you commit it; [Review generated diffs](/ambercast/how-to/review-generated-diffs/) shows how.

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="Configuration" href="/ambercast/reference/configuration/" description="See the grounding and ci configuration keys." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast run" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/run/" description="See every run flag, including --update-cache." />

<LinkCard title="Review generated diffs" href="/ambercast/how-to/review-generated-diffs/" description="Read the written-back diff before you commit it." />

# Review generated diffs
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/review-generated-diffs/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

List every changed file, read the prompt, then the plan, then the grounding, and finish with `check`.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

The resolver maps a prompt to its plan and grounding companions by fixed suffixes: `<name>.ambercast.plan.json` and `<name>.ambercast.grounding.json`.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## List the changed files \{#list-changes}

   ```bash
   git status --short
   ```

   For every untracked prompt, plan, or grounding path, read its full contents or run `git diff --no-index /dev/null <path>`. For changed tracked files, run `git diff -- <path>`, or `git diff HEAD -- <path>` when the file is staged. This fixes the complete candidate file set before you review meaning.

2. ## Review the prompt \{#review-prompt}

   Read `tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md` and state the intended user outcome. Prompt normalization changes only one leading BOM and the newline representation.

3. ## Review the plan \{#review-plan}

   Read `tests/ambercast/<name>.ambercast.plan.json` and compare the generated steps to that outcome. The plan is a separate derived companion.

4. ## Review the grounding \{#review-grounding}

   Read `tests/ambercast/<name>.ambercast.grounding.json` and tell a resolution change from an intent change. The grounding is a separate derived companion. With `grounding.repositoryPolicy` set to `uncommitted`, there may be no grounding file; skip this step then.

5. ## Check freshness \{#check-freshness}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast check tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md
   ```

   `check` has no write, browser, or provider capability.

</Steps>

## Verification \{#verification}

`check` exits `0` only after the accepted pair is fresh. With the `uncommitted` policy and no grounding file, it reports `fresh-without-grounding` and also exits `0`.

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="Plan document" href="/ambercast/spec/plan-document/" description="See the structure of a plan." />

<LinkCard title="Grounding document" href="/ambercast/spec/grounding-document/" description="See the structure of a grounding file." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast check" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/check/" description="See every check flag and result." />

<LinkCard title="File layout" href="/ambercast/reference/file-layout/" description="See where companion files live." />

<LinkCard title="Upgrade between versions" href="/ambercast/how-to/upgrade/" description="See how to handle plans after a version upgrade." />

---

# Manage artifacts in git
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/manage-artifacts-in-git/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Stage the prompt, plan, and grounding together, and keep the runs directory out of git.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

The default grounding policy is `repositoryPolicy: "committed"`. The default runs directory is `tests/ambercast/.runs`.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Stage the three files \{#stage-companions}

   With the `committed` policy, stage `<name>.test.md`, `<name>.ambercast.plan.json`, and `<name>.ambercast.grounding.json`. The resolver defines the two adjacent companion suffixes. See [File layout](/ambercast/reference/file-layout/#companions).

2. ## Ignore the run evidence \{#ignore-runs}

   Add the configured `runsDir` to `.gitignore`. For the default, add this line.

   ```text
   tests/ambercast/.runs/
   ```

   You can change `runsDir`. Each run writes one `report.json` in an invocation-specific directory below it.

3. ## Keep grounding local \{#keep-grounding-local}

   If grounding is a local cache, set `repositoryPolicy` to `uncommitted`. Do this step and the next one only in that case. The `$schema` value is the published configuration schema URL.

   ```json
   {"$schema":"https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/schemas/config.schema.json","grounding":{"repositoryPolicy":"uncommitted"}}
   ```

4. ## Ignore the local grounding \{#ignore-local-grounding}

   With `uncommitted`, also add this line to `.gitignore`. If your `testDir` differs from the default, replace `tests/ambercast` with it.

   ```text
   tests/ambercast/**/*.ambercast.grounding.json
   ```

   The resolver finds grounding companions only inside `testDir`, and only with the fixed `.ambercast.grounding.json` suffix. Plans stay tracked while the local grounding files are ignored.

</Steps>

## Verification \{#verification}

```bash
git status --short
```

- With `committed`, expect the plan and grounding companions.
- With `uncommitted`, expect the plan but no `testDir`-local `*.ambercast.grounding.json`.
- When the configured `runsDir` is ignored, expect no run evidence.

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="File layout" href="/ambercast/reference/file-layout/" description="See which files sit next to a prompt and where run evidence goes." />

<LinkCard title="Configuration" href="/ambercast/reference/configuration/" description="See configuration keys such as repositoryPolicy and runsDir." />

<LinkCard title="Plan document" href="/ambercast/spec/plan-document/" description="See the format of the plan file." />

<LinkCard title="Grounding document" href="/ambercast/spec/grounding-document/" description="See the format of the grounding file." />

<LinkCard title="Control grounding write-back" href="/ambercast/how-to/control-grounding-writeback/" description="Decide whether changed grounding is written back." />

# Run on other CI platforms
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/run-on-other-ci/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

In a job that already checks out your code, run `check` and then `run`, and leave healing and write-back off.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

You use GitLab CI or a generic runner, and the job has your code checked out. The flags of `run` include `--resolve`, `--update-cache`, `--allow-empty`, and `--list`, and `run` has no `--config` option.

The default behavior on a grounding miss already fails closed. CI needs no flag to suppress AI resolution.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Install Chromium \{#install-browser}

   Install the project's Node dependencies, then install Chromium. Cache the browser install directory with the platform's cache mechanism.

   ```bash
   npx playwright-core install chromium
   ```

   A replay of a fully grounded plan can proceed without selecting an AI provider.

2. ## Run check, then run \{#check-then-run}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast check && npx ambercast run
   ```

   The `&&` reaches `run` only when `check` exits `0`. `run` writes one report in its invocation directory.

3. ## Limit what you upload \{#limit-uploads}

   Step results in the report can retain `actual` text and an accessibility snapshot. Before you upload `report.json`, apply prior review, restricted access, and short retention. Upload it only when those controls are available.

   Upload invocation evidence or screenshots only by explicit opt-in, under the same controls. A failed live-browser step can save PNG screenshots in the invocation evidence directory.

   The safety scan cannot detect canvas, image, or CSS-rendered pixels. It also cannot detect changes between the scan and the screenshot.

4. ## Keep healing and write-back off \{#keep-heal-off}

   Do not invoke `heal`, and do not pass `--update-cache`. The CI defaults are `ci.heal: false` and `ci.updateGroundingCache: false`. Real healing in CI is an explicit opt-in through `ci.heal: true`.

</Steps>

## Verification \{#verification}

Gate the job on the process exit code. Untrustworthy artifacts (exit `4`) and environment failures (exit `3`) are distinct categories. See the [exit code table](/ambercast/reference/exit-codes/#exit-code-table).

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="Running ambercast in GitHub Actions" href="/ambercast/tutorials/github-actions/" description="Run the same flow in GitHub Actions." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast check" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/check/" description="See what check reports and when it exits non-zero." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast run" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/run/" description="See every flag of run." />

<LinkCard title="Exit codes" href="/ambercast/reference/exit-codes/" description="See the exit codes and their priority." />

<LinkCard title="Configuration" href="/ambercast/reference/configuration/" description="See configuration keys such as ci.heal and ci.updateGroundingCache." />

# Recover stale artifacts
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/recover-stale-artifacts/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Read the `check` status, take the action for that status, and run `check` again.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

`check` is read-only. It uses no provider, browser, event sink, or mutable storage.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Read the check status \{#read-status}

   ```bash
   npx ambercast check --json
   ```

   Find each reported status in the table in the next section.

2. ## Apply the action for that status \{#apply-action}

   Run the action in the status row. Replace `<name>` in a command with your prompt file name without the `.test.md` suffix, for example `login` for `login.test.md`.

3. ## Review the changes \{#review-changes}

   Before you commit a changed plan or grounding, read its diff. See [Review generated diffs](/ambercast/how-to/review-generated-diffs/).

</Steps>

## Status actions \{#stale}

| Status | Action | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fresh` | Run `npx ambercast check`. Change no artifact. | Exit `0`. |
| `fresh-without-grounding` | Run `npx ambercast generate tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md`. | `generate` repairs the adjacent grounding file on disk, then reports `skipped-fresh` with `planFile` only. `groundingFile` is not a generate result field. |
| `stale` | Run `npx ambercast generate tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md`, then read the diff. | A fresh generation can exit `0`. A check that is still untrustworthy exits `4`. |
| `missing-plan` | Restore the plan from version control, or run `npx ambercast generate tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md`. | The generate result has a `planFile`. |
| `missing-grounding` | Run `npx ambercast generate tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md`. | When the plan is fresh, `generate` creates the adjacent grounding file and returns `skipped-fresh` with `planFile` only. |
| `stale-grounding` | Run `npx ambercast generate tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md`, then read the new grounding. | When it is valid, check no longer reports a failed integrity finding. |
| `invalid-grounding` | Run `npx ambercast generate tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md`. If `check` still reports `invalid-grounding`, run `npx ambercast generate --force tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md`, which regenerates the plan and calls the AI provider, then read the new grounding. | When it is valid, check no longer reports a failed integrity finding. |
| `orphaned-plan` | Restore its prompt, or remove the orphan through the project's normal review process. | The next check no longer reports that orphan. |
| `orphaned-grounding` | Restore its prompt, or remove the orphan through the project's normal review process. | The next check no longer reports that orphan. |
| `invalid-artifact-name` | Rename or remove the invalid companion through normal review. | The next check no longer reports the artifact whose name cannot map back to a prompt. |
| `listed` | Run again without `--list`. | `--list` performed no plan or grounding read. |
| `skipped` | Run again after you resolve the interruption. | A run-scoped `INTERRUPTED` error contributes exit `3`. |

When the plan is fresh and its grounding is missing, does not parse, or has a different `planDigest`, the grounding that `generate` writes is an empty grounding bound to the plan. It is not a re-resolved one.

Bind the elements again on your machine with `npx ambercast run --resolve --update-cache tests/ambercast/<name>.test.md`, as step 3 of [Re-ground after a producer change](/ambercast/how-to/upgrade/#reground-after-producer-change) does.

## Verification \{#verification}

Run `npx ambercast check --json` again. It exits `0` only when no higher-priority candidate remains. See [aggregation priority](/ambercast/reference/exit-codes/#aggregation-priority).

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="ambercast check" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/check/" description="See the check statuses and the read-only contract." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast generate" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/generate/" description="See the generate results and exit codes." />

<LinkCard title="Error codes" href="/ambercast/reference/error-codes/" description="See every error code." />

<LinkCard title="Exit codes" href="/ambercast/reference/exit-codes/" description="See the exit codes and their priority." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast heal" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/heal/" description="See how heal repairs a drifted plan." />

<LinkCard title="Review generated diffs" href="/ambercast/how-to/review-generated-diffs/" description="Read changed plans and groundings before you commit." />

---

# Upgrade between versions
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/upgrade/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Read the BREAKING entries before you upgrade, then regenerate plans as `check` directs.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

A release whose BREAKING entry changes the producer fingerprint makes existing plans stale and requires regeneration. The 0.2.0 entry is an example: it names the `inputsDigest` impact. See the [changelog](/ambercast/reference/changelog/#release-020).

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Read the breaking changes \{#read-breaking}

   Read the target release's BREAKING section before you change the dependency.

2. ## Upgrade and run check \{#upgrade-and-check}

   Upgrade ambercast with your project's package manager, then run `check`. It returns a report and selects exit `4` for untrustworthy findings.

   ```bash
   npx ambercast check --json
   ```

3. ## Regenerate the stale plans \{#regenerate-stale}

   If `check` exits `4`, run `generate` and read the plan and grounding diff. See [Review generated diffs](/ambercast/how-to/review-generated-diffs/).

   ```bash
   npx ambercast generate
   ```

4. ## Commit together \{#commit-together}

   Commit the dependency and the accepted companion changes together. Then run `check` again so the final state is observable.

</Steps>

## Migrate secret grants \{#migrate-secret-grants}

Prompts created for Plan v2 can contain legacy secret grant lines. Remove every grant line from the prompt. The old syntax is rejected and must not be migrated in place.

```markdown
@ambercast-secret {{secrets.password}}
```

Then run `npx ambercast generate --force <file>` and answer the new consent prompt. For CI or another non-interactive environment, add the reviewed names to `secrets.allow` first. The regenerated plan uses the v3 consent and allowlist model.

## Re-ground after a producer change \{#reground-after-producer-change}

Changes to generator instructions or the response contract change the producer fingerprint, so plans from earlier releases are stale. Regenerating a plan replaces its grounding with an empty one, and the steps below bind every element step again. Plan 5 and Grounding 4 are unchanged.

Report 3.11 adds `generator-assumption` warnings and optional `warnings` on `healed` rows. Update your report schema if you validate a closed union.

The CLI `--strict` flag and the MCP `strict` argument have been removed. Remove them from your calls. `ambercast generate --strict` exits 2 as an unknown option, and MCP rejects `strict` during input validation.

1. Run `npx ambercast check --json` and confirm that the affected plans report `stale`.
2. Run `npx ambercast generate <file>` for each stale plan. In the diff, check that each assert lists in its `confirms` the inputs whose effects it shows.
   - If generate warns `action-unconfirmed` for an input, do not go on to step 3.
   - A plain run fails on that input with `GROUNDING_UNRESOLVED`.
   - Add an assert that shows the effect of that input, such as the signed-in user name, and repeat step 2.
3. Run `npx ambercast run --resolve --update-cache <file>` on your machine. The grounding is empty after regeneration, so ambercast calls AI once for each element step that has no verbatim quote. CI does not save the grounding by default.
4. Run `npx ambercast check` and confirm that the plan is `fresh`. Then run `npx ambercast run <file>` and confirm that it passes and that `aiCalls` is 0 in the report.
   - Always commit the plan.
   - Commit the grounding with it only when `grounding.repositoryPolicy` is `committed`.
   - When it is `uncommitted`, keep the grounding local.

## Verification \{#verification}

After you accept the regeneration, `npx ambercast check` exits `0`.

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="Changelog" href="/ambercast/reference/changelog/" description="Read the BREAKING entries of each release." />

<LinkCard title="Freshness and digests" href="/ambercast/spec/freshness/" description="See when a plan counts as stale." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast check" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/check/" description="See the check statuses and exit codes." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast generate" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/generate/" description="See the generate results and exit codes." />

<LinkCard title="Review generated diffs" href="/ambercast/how-to/review-generated-diffs/" description="Read regenerated plans and groundings before you commit." />

# Troubleshoot common failures
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/troubleshoot/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Keep the failing command's output, take the action for the matching symptom, and re-run the smallest affected command.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

Your command invocation must be valid. Invalid flags, malformed command arguments, and missing option values write usage to stderr and exit `2` without a report envelope.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Find the matching symptom \{#match-symptom}

   Keep the failing command's output. Re-run it with `--json` when you need the report. Find the matching symptom in the table in the next section.

2. ## Apply the action \{#apply-action}

   Take the action in that row. Use [Error codes](/ambercast/reference/error-codes/) for the exact error vocabulary and [Exit codes](/ambercast/reference/exit-codes/#priority) for process-status values and priority.

3. ## Re-run the smallest command \{#rerun-smallest}

   Re-run the smallest affected command.

</Steps>

## Symptoms and actions \{#symptom-table}

| Symptom | Cause | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Invalid config, unresolved secret, or target | A configuration or invocation boundary needs correction. | Read [Error codes](/ambercast/reference/error-codes/), then correct the named setting without guessing values. |
| Missing, stale, or untrustworthy companion | The committed artifact cannot be used as current evidence. | Use the matching row in [Recover stale artifacts](/ambercast/how-to/recover-stale-artifacts/). |
| `SECRET_CONSENT_REQUIRED` | Generation found a secret name that is not on the allowlist, and consent was declined or unavailable. | Review the name and add it to `secrets.allow`, or run generate again interactively. Do not add a secret value to the prompt. |
| Heal reports `secret-set-changed` | A Stage 3 candidate changed the complete secret-name set, which heal cannot reattribute or consent to silently. | Run `ambercast generate --force <file>` and complete consent. The CLI prints this hint with the actual file path in place of `<file>`: `秘匿値の構成が変わった。ambercast generate --force <file> で再生成し同意を取り直す` |
| Literal secret or legacy secret syntax | Protected IR rejected a secret-handling boundary. | Use [Manage secrets](/ambercast/how-to/manage-secrets/). Do not place a literal or a legacy grant line in the prompt. |
| Browser, provider, storage, or crash | The execution environment failed. | Keep the output, repair the environment, then re-run the smallest command. |
| Interrupted work | Batch work was incomplete. | Re-run after you resolve the interruption. |
| Failed assertion | A replayed case has failing evidence. | Read the report, fix the app or the prompt, then re-run. |
| Empty selection | No prompt matched the requested selection. | Correct the selection, or use `--allow-empty` only when the selection is meant to be empty. |

## Verification \{#verification}

Re-run the smallest affected command. It exits `0` only after no higher-priority condition remains.

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="Error codes" href="/ambercast/reference/error-codes/" description="See the exact error vocabulary." />

<LinkCard title="Exit codes" href="/ambercast/reference/exit-codes/" description="See the exit codes and their priority." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast check" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/check/" description="See the check statuses." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast generate" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/generate/" description="See the generate results." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast run" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/run/" description="See the flags and results of run." />

<LinkCard title="ambercast heal" href="/ambercast/reference/cli/heal/" description="See how heal behaves and what it reports." />

<LinkCard title="Recover stale artifacts" href="/ambercast/how-to/recover-stale-artifacts/" description="See the action for each check status." />

<LinkCard title="Manage secrets" href="/ambercast/how-to/manage-secrets/" description="Approve secret names and pass their values." />

<LinkCard title="Configure targets" href="/ambercast/how-to/configure-targets/" description="Set up targets and the related configuration." />

# Contribute
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/how-to/contribute/

import { Steps, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

As an external contributor, open an issue, fork and branch, run three checks, and open a pull request.

## Prerequisites \{#prerequisites}

The package declares the `npm test`, `npm run typecheck`, and `npm run lint` scripts.

## Steps \{#steps}

<Steps>

1. ## Open an issue \{#open-issue}

   Open an issue that describes the problem or proposal.

2. ## Fork and branch \{#fork-and-branch}

   Fork the repository and create a branch for your change.

3. ## Run the three checks \{#run-checks}

   ```bash
   npm test
   npm run typecheck
   npm run lint
   ```

4. ## Open a pull request \{#open-pull-request}

   Open a pull request with a Conventional Commit title, and resolve its review conversations.

</Steps>

## Report a vulnerability \{#report-vulnerability}

Report a vulnerability through GitHub Security Advisories, not a public issue. Send a private report with the version, a reproduction, and the impact. See the [security policy](/ambercast/reference/security-policy/).

## Maintainer and agent workflow \{#maintainer-workflow}

`AGENTS.md` and `.claude/` describe the maintainer's AI-agent automation. They are not prerequisites for external contributors, and external pull request checks run in CI.

A maintainer or repository agent follows the development workflow in `AGENTS.md`, including its behavior-change test order.

## Verification \{#verification}

The three package commands exit `0`, or their failure is documented before handoff. Confirm that your pull request is open.

## Related \{#related}

<LinkCard title="Security policy" href="/ambercast/reference/security-policy/" description="See how to report a vulnerability and what to expect." />

<LinkCard title="Changelog" href="/ambercast/reference/changelog/" description="See the changes of each release." />

# Configuration
Source: https://kotarotsubaki.github.io/ambercast/reference/configuration/

ambercast builds its configuration from one configuration file and built-in defaults. This page covers how it picks the file, the target settings, and every key.

## File selection {#file-selection}

A configuration file that is present must contain `$schema`. Every other declared key is optional.

ambercast chooses the file in this order:

1. The `--config` value on the command. `generate`, `check`, and `view` accept it. `run`, `heal`, `init`, and `mcp` do not. See the [command flag matrix](/ambercast/reference/cli/overview/#command-flag-matrix).
2. The `AMBERCAST_CONFIG` variable, described in [Environment variables](/ambercast/reference/environment-variables/#configuration).
3. An `ambercast.config.json` in an ancestor directory.
4. The built-in defaults.

An explicit path that does not exist is an error. It does not fall through to discovery or the defaults.

A `targets` object you supply replaces the default targets instead of merging with them. If the replacement omits `defaultTarget`, the default is cleared.

## Targets {#targets}

A target supplies a web surface and a browser destination. ambercast resolves `healReplayIsolation` and `resolveTimeoutMs` live, before heal and before element resolution. They are not plan fields and do not enter `inputsDigest`.

When it loads the file, ambercast canonicalizes an authored `locale` with `Intl.getCanonicalLocales`. For example, `"ja-jp"` becomes `"ja-JP"`. A value that throws `RangeError`, an empty string, or a non-string fails with `CONFIG_INVALID` (exit 2) at issue path `targets.<name>.locale`.

The normalized locale reaches the plan's target definition and the Playwright browser context. It affects `navigator.language` and the `Accept-Language` header of the first request for that target's pages.

The setting stops there. It does not set the timezone, an application-side language cookie, or an application preference. It also defines no priority against those mechanisms.

## Key table {#key-table}

| key path | type | default | constraint | consumers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `$schema` | string | — | required in a present file | loader |
| `testDir` | string | `tests/ambercast` | resolves to an absolute layout path | generate, run, check, heal (discovery and layout) |
| `runsDir` | string | `tests/ambercast/.runs` | resolves to an absolute layout path | run (reports and evidence); heal (contained writes) |
| `testMatch` | string[] | `["**/*.test.md"]` | limited `*`/`**` matcher. Every pattern must end in `.test.md`, or loading fails with `CONFIG_INVALID` | generate, run, check, heal (discovery) |
| `testIgnore` | string[] | `["**/.runs/**","**/*.ambercast.plan.json","**/*.ambercast.grounding.json"]` | excludes after inclusion match | generate, run, check, heal (discovery) |
| `secrets.allow` | `SecretName[] \| "*"` | `[]` | an empty array requires consent for every secret name. `"*"` allows every name without consent (not recommended). A non-empty array allows exactly those names | generate, run, heal |
| `targets.<name>.baseUrl` | string | `http://localhost:3000` on `web-user` | required in every target you write; an http(s) URL without a literal `{{secrets.`. Replaces the whole target record | generate (input); run, check, heal (plan-referenced targets) |
| `targets.<name>.surface` | `web` | absent | only `web` in TP1. The optional field resolves to `web` at use, not through a schema default | generate; plan target definition |
| `targets.<name>.description` | string | absent | optional generation context | generate |
| `targets.<name>.executor.kind` | `playwright` | `playwright` | live UI executor kind; excluded from the plan digest | run, heal (executor composition) |
| `targets.<name>.executor.browser` | `chromium` | `chromium` | live executor browser; excluded from the plan digest | run, heal (executor composition) |
| `targets.<name>.secretSinkOrigins` | `Record<SecretRef, SecretSinkOrigin[]>` | absent | an absent secret entry permits only `baseUrl`. An empty array denies that secret everywhere. A non-empty array replaces that default. Each origin is `scheme://host[:port]` with port 1–65535, and has no path, query, fragment, wildcard, userinfo, or literal `{{secrets.` | generate, run, heal (secret sink policy); check (freshness) |
| `targets.<name>.healReplayIsolation` | `idempotent\|stateful` | `stateful` | heal requires every plan-referenced target to be `idempotent` | heal |
| `targets.<name>.locale` | string | absent | canonicalized with `Intl.getCanonicalLocales`. A value that fails canonicalization is `CONFIG_INVALID` | generate; plan target definition; run (browser context) |
| `targets.<name>.resolveTimeoutMs` | integer | `5000` | 0–60000 | run, heal |
| `defaultTarget` | string | `web-user` | must resolve to a target. The generator uses it when the prompt does not identify a step's target | generate |
| `ai.provider` | `claude\|codex\|auto` | `auto` | a CLI flag or environment variable may override it | generate; run (fallback); heal |
| `ai.maxGenerateAttempts` | positive integer | `2` | 1–5; generation attempts per file | generate only; never heal Stage 3 |
| `ai.timeoutMs` | positive integer | `600000` | positive | generate; run (fallback); heal |
| `viewer.port` | integer | `4600` | 1–65535; the starting candidate, overridden by `--port` | view |
| `ci.heal` | boolean | `false` | opt-in to non-list heal in CI | heal |
| `ci.updateGroundingCache` | boolean | `false` | opt-in to cache write-back in CI | run |
| `grounding.repositoryPolicy` | `committed\|uncommitted` | `committed` | finite vocabulary | check |
| `grounding.localWriteBack` | `auto\|explicit` | `auto` | ignored in CI | run |
| `heal.maxStepRepairs` | positive integer | absent | caps incremental real-provider dispatches only | heal |
| `heal.caseTimeoutMs` | positive integer | `300000` | case admission deadline | heal |

The `testMatch` and `testIgnore` patterns follow the [pattern language](/ambercast/reference/discovery-patterns/#pattern-language).

## Secret consent {#secret-consent}

`secrets.allow` is the durable allowlist of logical secret names found during generation. `generate` prompts for any name outside a list value and merges the names you accept into the file. In CI or another non-interactive context, fill the list with names that were already reviewed.

`"*"` skips per-name consent and accepts any name the AI proposes. It is a high-risk escape hatch, not a safer default. Use it only when you intend to accept arbitrary proposed names without review.

## AI configuration {#ai}

`ai.maxGenerateAttempts` is the maximum number of provider attempts per prompt during `generate`, including the first attempt. `generate` tries again only when local validation rejects a response. The range is 1 to 5, and the default is 2. It never applies to heal repairs.

`ai.timeoutMs` is the deadline in milliseconds for one provider dispatch, with a default of 600000. It applies to every generate, run, and heal dispatch. The heal case deadline only decides admission, so an admitted dispatch can still run up to this value.

## Healing configuration {#heal}

`heal.maxStepRepairs` caps incremental real-provider dispatches. `heal.caseTimeoutMs` is the admission deadline for the whole case.

## Grounding write-back {#grounding}

| environment | resolved policy | grounding writes when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| local | `localWriteBack: auto` | a grounding result changed |
| local | `localWriteBack: explicit` | `--update-cache` is passed |
| CI | `localWriteBack` ignored | `--update-cache` is passed or `ci.updateGroundingCache: true` |

See [ambercast run](/ambercast/reference/cli/run/#grounding-write-back) for the command behavior.

## See also {#see-also}

- [CLI overview](/ambercast/reference/cli/overview/#command-flag-matrix)
- [Discovery patterns](/ambercast/reference/discovery-patterns/#pattern-language)
- [Environment variables](/ambercast/reference/environment-variables/#configuration)
- [ambercast run](/ambercast/reference/cli/run/#grounding-write-back)
